summary: Johann III Bernoulli was a scholar in history, archaeology, and other fields who studied at the University of Basel (~1757–1758) and University of Neuchâtel (~1758–1762). He held memberships at the Prussian Academy of Sciences, Imperial Academy of Sciences, and Naturforschende Gesellschaft in Danzig.
Philosopher Johann Jakob Engel studied at the University of Rostock (~1759–1762) and Leipzig University (~1762–1765). He later taught Wilhelm von Humboldt.

Working in history and archaeology, Johann Joachim Winckelmann studied at Köllnisches Gymnasium in 1736, Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg from 1738 to 1740, and the University of Jena from 1741 to 1742.

Johann Tobias Beck, a scholar of religious studies and philosophy, studied at the University of Tübingen (~1822–1826). He later held posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).

Indologist and scholar Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff studied at the University of Tübingen and Tübinger Stift. He held posts at Tübinger Stift, Melanchthon-Gymnasium Nürnberg, University of Tartu/Imperial University of Dorpat, University of Würzburg, and Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg.

Indologist and archaeologist Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw studied at Leiden University and Utrecht University under Jan Gonda. She held posts at Cambridge, the University of Groningen, and the University of Amsterdam, and founded the Ancient India & Iran Trust.

Working in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, Johanna Narten studied under Ernst Zinn at Saarland University and Karl Hoffmann at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg. She was an Assistentin at Erlangen-Nürnberg and a member of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities.

Johannes Beltz, a scholar of Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies, completed his PhD studies at the University of Lausanne and École Pratique des Hautes Études by 1999 under Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst.

Johannes Bronkhorst, a scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy, studied at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, University of Rajasthan, Savitribai Phule Pune University under Shivram Dattatray Joshi, and Leiden University. He served as a professor at the University of Lausanne from 1987 to 2025.

Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis was a scholar of history, archaeology, Indology, and linguistics who studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939). He later served on the faculties of SOAS University of London (~1964–1986) and Leiden University (1978–1986).

Indologist Johannes Hertel earned his doctorate at Leipzig University (1892–1897). He taught at Lessing-Gymnasium Döbeln (~1898–1920) and held the chair of Indian philology at Leipzig University from 1919 to 1937.

Indologist Johannes Klatt studied under Albrecht Weber and completed a doctorate at the University of Halle / Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1869–1873). From 1872 onward, he served as a staff member, assistant, custodian, and librarian at the Prussian State Library.

Johannes Nobel, a scholar of Indology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology, studied at Greifswald and Berlin under Heinrich Lüders. He worked at the Prussian State Library, lectured at Humboldt University of Berlin, and held the Indology chair at the University of Marburg (1928–1955).

Johannes Rahder, a scholar in Buddhist studies, Japanology, and Indology, earned his doctorate at Utrecht University (~1920–1926). He held professorships at Utrecht University, Leiden University (1931–1946), the University of Hawaiʻi, and Yale University (1947–1965).

Linguist and Indologist Johannes Schmidt studied at the University of Bonn under Ritschl and Jahn, at Jena under August Schleicher, and under Albrecht Weber. He held posts at the University of Bonn, University of Graz (1873–1876), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1876).

Indologist and Tibetologist Johannes Schneider studied at the University of Marburg (1986–1992). He held posts at the Free University of Berlin, Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities, and University of Munich, where he became an außerplanmäßiger Professor in 2014.

Johannes Schubert studied Tibetology and Sinology at Leipzig University and under scholars including Conrady, Francke, and Haenisch. He worked at Leipzig University Library (~1927–1954), the Ahnenerbe (~1938–1945), and taught Tibetan and Mongolian at Leipzig University across 1934–1962.

John A. Ardussi, a scholar in Tibetology and history and archaeology, studied under Turrell V. Wylie for his MA and earned a PhD from the Australian National University (attested 1977). He has served on a research team at the CNRS.

John Alexander Jorgensen, a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology, earned his MA at the Australian National University under Kenneth Herbert Joseph Gardiner in 1979. He later held posts at ANU and Griffith University.

John Alexander Stewart, who worked in linguistics and other fields, studied at the University of Aberdeen (~1899–1903). He served in the Indian Civil Service (~1905–1933) and later taught at the University of London and SOAS (~1933–1948).
